primary_meaning: In Christian teaching and biblical interpretation, 'fornication' or 'whoredom' (Hebrew zanah/zenut; Greek porneia) used symbolically refers to spiritual unfaithfulness to God — most specifically idolatry and apostasy. Because the covenant between God and His people is portrayed as a marriage, worshiping other gods, trusting foreign alliances, or mixing pagan practices with true worship is depicted as adultery or prostitution against the divine Husband. The unfaithful people (Israel, Judah, or apostate 'Babylon') are personified as a harlot.
primary_basis: Hosea 1–3 (Hosea commanded to marry a 'wife of whoredoms' because 'the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD,' Hos 1:2)
Ezekiel 16 (Jerusalem as an unfaithful wife who 'playedst the harlot' with idols and foreign nations)
Ezekiel 23 (Oholah and Oholibah, Samaria and Jerusalem, as harlot sisters)
Jeremiah 3:1–10, 20 ('thou hast played the harlot with many lovers'; Israel's 'whoredoms' under every green tree)
Exodus 34:15–16 ('go a whoring after their gods')
Judges 2:17; 8:27, 33 (Israel 'went a whoring after other gods' / after the ephod and Baalim)
Isaiah 1:21 ('How is the faithful city become an harlot!')
Revelation 17:1–5 (the great whore, 'Babylon the Great, the Mother of Harlots,' with whom the kings of the earth committed fornication)
Revelation 2:14, 20–22 (Balaam and Jezebel linking fornication with idolatry in the churches)
James 4:4 ('ye adulterers and adulteresses... friendship of the world is enmity with God')

alternatives.meaning: Literal sexual immorality: porneia and 'fornication' frequently carry their plain, non-symbolic sense of illicit sexual activity (e.g., 1 Cor 6:18; 1 Thess 4:3; Acts 15:20). Many interpreters insist the literal meaning is primary in ethical texts and only becomes figurative in prophetic/apocalyptic contexts.

Political and commercial alliance / illicit dependence on worldly powers: the harlotry imagery (especially of Tyre in Isaiah 23:15–17 and Babylon in Revelation 17–18) is read as denoting corrupt political entanglement, economic exploitation, and trafficking with the kings and merchants of the earth rather than idolatry narrowly defined.
basis: Revelation 18:3, 9–19 (kings and merchants enriched by the harlot)

alternatives.meaning: Identification of the symbolic whore/fornication with a specific apostate religious system: historicist Protestant interpretation classically identified the whore of Revelation 17 with the Roman Catholic Church / papal Rome, so 'fornication' meant church-state union and doctrinal corruption. Preterist and many modern scholars instead identify her with pagan Rome or first-century Jerusalem.
basis: Revelation 18:4 ('Come out of her, my people')

alternatives.meaning: Cultic/ritual prostitution reading: some scholars have argued the prophetic 'whoredom' language originally referenced actual Canaanite fertility-cult prostitution practiced by Israelites, so the term is partly literal in Hosea and Ezekiel; more recent scholarship questions the historical existence of widespread cult prostitution and treats the language as purely metaphorical.

Broadened covenantal reading: 'fornication' as any breach of covenant loyalty or worldliness generally — friendship with the world, materialism, or divided allegiance — not restricted to formal idol worship.

notes: This is one of the most firmly established symbolic equations in biblical interpretation: when used figuratively, fornication/whoredom = unfaithfulness to God, chiefly idolatry/apostasy, grounded in the marriage metaphor for the covenant. The consensus spans patristic, medieval, Reformation, and modern critical scholarship. Disagreement is not over whether this symbolism exists but over (a) when a given passage is literal versus figurative, and (b) the specific historical referent of the harlot in Revelation 17 (papal Rome, pagan Rome, Jerusalem, or a generic world system). The last point is where confessional traditions diverge most sharply.
